title: Development of functional genomic technologies in mice
text:
Functional genomic technologies have been developed primary in cultured cells making it difficult to address
the complex phenotypes, such as spatial-temporal, and tissue/cell type specificity and interactions that occur in
organisms. In this proposal, I will combine zygote manipulation methods and functional genomics technologies
to develop novel high-throughput assays in mice, including MPRA and large-scale CRISPR saturation
mutagenesis. The novel in vivo high-throughput technologies that I will develop in my training phase will enable
to study in mice regulatory elements and disease-associated variants at developmental time points and tissues
in my independent stage.

title: Short-wave infrared Cerenkov imaging to better visualize targeted radiotherapy and diagnostic radiotracers
text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE & PUBLIC HEALTH RELEVANCE STATEMENT
Cerenkov luminescence imaging (CLI) provides an opportunity to provide facile and cheaper imaging of
radiotracers, including targeted radiotherapy, particularly with alpha and electron emitters, which are very
difficult to image otherwise, however, currently CLI is severely limited by the requirement to image in total
darkness. Our application provides a novel imaging paradigm for CLI in ambient light with unprecedented
sensitivity and signal penetration, making Cerenkov imaging overall more accessible and an option to monitor
therapy with alpha-emitting isotopes.

title: Functional evolution of segmentation gene regulatory networks in insects
text:
Regulatory genes that control embryonic development are shared among diverse species because changes in
their basic functions are highly deleterious. Surprisingly, we found that the genes controlling a fundamental
feature of the insect body plan – segmentation – have changed during insect evolution, with genes gained, lost
or changed in function. We explore the evolutionary and molecular mechanisms underlying these changes,
which have allowed for seamless re-wiring of regulatory interactions, and develop tools to examine a cohort of
segmentation genes in new insect model systems that use different genes for early patterning than the
established model Drosophila melanogaster.

title: High-throughput and Machine Learning Optimization of Fluorescent Sensors for Multiplexed Imaging in vivo
text:
Genetically-encoded, fluorescent protein sensors would provide tremendous advantages for analyzing
highly heterogeneous neuronal activity in the brain, but engineering and validation pioneering sensors only occur
in incremental steps. We aim to significantly accelerate the engineering of sensors for calcium and
neuromodulator detection by utilizing a novel high-throughput platform and machine learning, enabling the
functional testing of large variant libraries at orders-of-magnitude accelerated speeds. The efficient engineering
of precise and fully validated sensors will allow neuroscientists and biomedical researchers to precisely detect
the timing and location of neuronal signals and hence, could guide future neuroscience research on disease
mechanisms, facilitate drug screening, and help to develop novel therapeutic approaches.

title: Developing novel botulism antidotes and a platform for intra-neuronal delivery of nanobodies
text:
Botulinum neurotoxins (BoNTs) are extremely potent bacterial toxins causing the paralytic botulism syndrome.
We propose to develop a platform for intra-neuronal delivery of nanobodies in order to neutralize the toxin inside
the intoxicated neurons and accelerate recovery of botulism. The accomplishment of our goals will result in novel
antidotes to treat post-exposure botulism, as well as a versatile platform for delivery of protein therapeutics to
act on other intra-neuronal targets.

title: Genetics and Developmental Biology Training Program
text:
This grant supports innovative training of 14 Ph.D. students in Genetics and Developmental Biology at
Stanford University, an interdisciplinary program that bridges different departments and prepares our students
to carry out innovative, rigorous research and become leaders in academia and industry. Outstanding faculty
and trainees combine new methods and diverse study systems to advance our mechanistic understanding of
genes, cells, tissues, organs, organisms, and human health and disease. These advances have spurred on the
biotechnology and biopharmaceutical industries that have ultimately led to improved clinical care and health
outcome for millions of patients.

title: Genetic Strategies for Neurodevelopmental Research
text:
To better understand the neurobiological and molecular underpinnings of autism spectrum disorder, a
first goal of this application is to develop a nonhuman primate model through genetic modification of the
CHD8 gene. This gene is among the most frequently mutated genes in individuals with ASD. A long-
term goal is to establish infrastructure to enable the generation of genetically modified monkeys for
translational biomedical research - which we believe to be in the national interest.

title: PROX1-dependent epigenetic regulation of phenotypic plasticity during colorectal cancer metastasis
text:
Metastasis causes death by acquiring the unique ability to disseminate from a primary tumor and to adapt to
foreign microenvironments. In colorectal cancer (CRC) and other solid cancers, metastatic progression is
characterized by dedifferentiation into more primitive fetal states preceding a gain in phenotypic plasticity and
the emergence of transdifferentiated cell states. The goal of this proposal is to test the hypothesis that PROX1,
a transcriptional co-repressor aberrantly expressed during fetal reversion in CRC, modulates transcriptional
and epigenetic programs that license phenotypic plasticity in metastasis.

title: Novel Computational Methods for Microbiome Data Analysis in Longitudinal Study
text:
To enhance understanding the microbiome's dynamic role in disease progression, and explore its clinical
potential, we will develop two sets of analytic methods designed to 1) detect genome-wide microbial variants,
identify strains within species, and estimate strain relative abundance using longitudinal metagenomics samples
and 2) develop, validate, and apply the microbial risk scores in disease prediction. Further, we will validate the
proposed tools in multiple longitudinal microbiome studies; explore new insights; and develop, distribute, and
support open-source software packages to apply the tools.

title: Bidirectional signaling in T cell differentiation
text:
Statement
T cells are the cornerstone for immunotherapies for cancer and other diseases, but there is limited understanding
of mechanisms coordinately regulating the antitumor function of CD8+ T cells and bidirectional tumor–immune
crosstalk. We reveal Ube2l3, an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme, as a crucial negative regulator of CD8+ T cell
antitumor function and tumor–immune interactions. A better understanding of these pathways, using both
candidate and screening approaches, is essential for our efforts to develop next-generation immunotherapeutic
strategies.

title: Sulfide metabolism and signaling
text:
Hydrogen sulfide is paradigmatic of the rich interplay between host and gut microbial metabolism that is
influenced by diet, and in turn, influences whole-body sulfide homeostasis. Our laboratory has been at the
forefront of deciphering how sulfide, by reversibly poisoning respiration, also remodels host redox and energy
metabolism. In the next cycle, our studies will illuminate how host sulfide metabolism is regulated, and reveal
the molecular underpinnings of its intersections with oxygen metabolism in the context of normal physiology and
disease.

title: Integrated Genomics Core
text: INTEGRATED GENOMICS CORE | PROJECT SUMMARY The aim of the CLEAR Consortium’s Integrated Genomics Core is to facilitate synergy between the different projects and accelerate the program by providing a comprehensive, cost effective and highly integrated suite of genomic services used by all three Projects. Project 1 performs genome/exom sequencing of patient-parent trios to identify putative TED-causing variants, and has established the CLEAR registry a database that integrates genomic and clinical data. Projects 2 and 3 will perform experiments with single cells RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analyses to define the genomic basis of normal and disrupted TE development in animal models and human iPSC-derived organoids. The Core will used state-of-the-art bioinformatics, computational and statistical methods to analyze and integrate of all this genomic data. The core provides statistical rigor, supports bioinformatics literacy of the wet bench teams, provides data management, and facilitates data sharing between the projects and broader scientific community.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Dashboard Tools to Collect, Anonymize, and Summarize Companion Animal Antimicrobial Use Data
text:
Antimicrobial resistant bacteria are a growing public health threat that can spread among animals and people
and are caused by using antimicrobials, whether in people or companion animals, such as dogs, cats, and
horses. Therefore, it is important to monitor antimicrobial use and trends in all species, but we have limited
information on antimicrobial use in companion animals because it is time intensive to gather from veterinary
records. Our approach uses novel artificial intelligence and dashboards to efficiently extract and analyze
anonymous antimicrobial use information from veterinary records, filling a gap in our understanding and
ultimately promoting judicious use of antimicrobials.

title: An Interneuron-based Cell Therapy for Epilepsy
text:
Epilepsy is a common neurological disorder afflicting nearly 3 million Americans. Given that loss or reduction of
inhibitory synaptic transmission in hippocampus is one potential mechanism resulting in emergence of epilepsy,
a method to generate new hippocampal interneurons could have direct therapeutic consequences. Using porcine
embryonic neural progenitor cells and rodent model of temporal lobe epilepsy or epilepsy-autism disorder we
propose to develop a novel interneuron-based cell therapy.

title: Cellular Programming in Persistent Versus Lytic Viral Infections
text: CELLULAR REPROGRAMMING IN PERSISTENT VS. LYTIC VIRAL INFECTIONS PROJECT SUMMARY The long-range goal of the proposed research is to define the cellular factors that mediate JC polyomavirus (JCPyV) infection to better understand how virus-host cell interactions influence viral pathogenesis. JCPyV infects up to 80% of the population and establishes a lifelong, asymptomatic persistent infection in the kidneys of healthy individuals. However, in immunocompromised individuals JCPyV can spread to the central nervous system (CNS) and cause a lytic infection in glial cells resulting in the fatal, demyelinating disease progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Approximately 5% of individuals with HIV develop PML, a terminal AIDS- defining illness, and individuals receiving immunomodulatory therapies for diseases including multiple sclerosis are at heightened risk for PML development. The increasing number of individuals receiving immunomodulatory therapies due to immune-mediated diseases has led to a rising number of PML cases in the past decade. Over 700 total cases of PML are due to a single drug class. PML can be fatal, especially when underlying immunosuppression is left untreated, and there are currently no approved treatments for this devastating disease. The lack of an animal model and limited cell culture models have largely restricted studies of JCPyV to a single transformed cell culture model. Recently-published studies have revealed that primary cell culture models are a better representation of disease pathogenesis in vivo, and thus we have developed innovative primary cell culture models to define cellular factors that are required for JCPyV infection. Two integrated specific aims are proposed in this research project to: 1) characterize cellular factors that mediate JCPyV entry and infection in primary cell types, and 2) elucidate cell-type dependent differences in persistent and lytic JCPyV infections. This research will enhance our understanding of how virus-host cell interactions influence disease outcomes and will serve as a platform for the development of antiviral treatments. Through this work, cellular factors required for JCPyV entry in primary cell types will be characterized through loss- and gain-of-function approaches using cell-based assays. Transcriptome profiling through RNA sequencing analysis will be used to determine how JCPyV infection alters gene expression in a cell-type dependent manner to identify pathways relevant to JCPyV pathogenesis and fatal disease outcomes. This combinatorial approach utilizes newly developed primary cell models of JCPyV infection and takes advantage of innovative high-throughput analysis of viral and cellular protein expression and RNA sequencing approaches. This research will fill key gaps in our knowledge of JCPyV biology and could elucidate novel antiviral targets or provide rationale for experimental use of on-market therapies to prevent or treat the fatal disease PML. Findings obtained from this research will also provide broader insights into the entry and signaling networks for other pathogenic viruses, like coronaviruses, and improve our understanding of dysregulation of cellular signaling in other diseases such as cancer.

title: PhysioSim: Innovative Physiology Simulation Education Kits for Pre-College Students and Teachers
text:
Evidence shows that activities promoting active learning rather than passive lectures improve students’ pursuit
and persistence in STEM careers – most significantly for underrepresented students. While the introduction of
STEM educational products has been working to increase the number of students pursuing careers in science,
technology, engineering, and math, the health science area has been underserved. A product that provides
students with hands-on activities and experience in health science-related fields may increase interest and the
belief that they can successfully pursue healthcare-related careers.

title: Immune Monitoring Shared Resource
text: IMMUNE MONITORING SHARED RESOURCE: ABSTRACT The study of cellular phenotypes and states within complex biological networks, such as the human immune system, is crucial to the advancement of cancer medicine. Although various tools are available to support this research, significant barriers, such as high costs, complexity in data acquisition, and specialized analytical pipelines often hinder access. The Immune Monitoring Shared Resource (IMSR) was created to provide Mayo Clinic researchers, including Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center (MCCCC) members, with comprehensive access to high-dimensional single-cell tools. This initiative aims to accelerate basic, translational, and clinical research by leveraging state-of-the-art technology and advanced expertise to study complex biological systems. These functions are enacted through three Specific Aims: Aim 1: Support high-parameter analysis of single-cell suspensions generated from complex biological systems (high-dimensional cytometry). This service uses cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF). Aim 2: Support high-parameter spatial analysis of single-cell data generated from intact tissue sections (high-dimensional spatial biology). Imaging mass cytometry or multiplex immunofluorescence are used to provide this service. Aim 3: Develop, test, validate, and share bioinformatic tools to support analysis of complex datasets generated by using these systems. Close collaboration with the Mayo Clinic Bioinformatics Shared Resource is used to provide this service. The IMSR is an enterprise-wide core that operates under a full-service philosophy, providing MCCCC members with an end-to-end solution that includes project consultations, sample preparation, data acquisition, and data analysis. Member Utilization 2019-2023: 66 Total (1 CPCS, 3 REDI, 11 CGSM, 20 CII, 10 NTTM, 21 ACTS) Publication by Members: 18, 13 with Impact Factor >10

title: Molecular Imaging Probe(s) for Optical Surgical Navigation of Pancreatic Cancer
text:
Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a highly lethal malignancy with surgical resection as the most effective curative option.
Limited sensitivities of pre-operative imaging modalities, inconspicuous lesion/margin detection under white light,
and limited efficacy of surgical Laparoscopy to visualize small lesions contribute to incomplete resections, high
local recurrence rates, and poor outcomes. We propose to develop and evaluate MUC4-targeted near-infrared
fluorescence imaging probes to facilitate fluorescence-guided surgical navigation for improved surgical resection
of PC and its pre-malignant precursor lesions.

title: Navigation assistance using multimodal LLM and computer vision
text:
The proposed research aims to address the micro-navigation need, which is still largely unmet as the GPS-
based navigation solutions do not have pin-point accuracy and fail in GPS-denied areas. To address the
independent travel need, the proposed solution uses the latest AI and computer vision technologies. The
research will contribute to the missions of NEI to support research with respect to blinding eye diseases and
visual disorders.

title: Multicenter Validation for a Deep Learning Approach for Enhanced Urine Cytological Assessment and Rapid Bladder Cancer Screening
text:
Although bladder cancer is one of the most common and recurrent cancers worldwide, current noninvasive
diagnostic methods are inconsistent and inefficient, making screening frequent, costly, and challenging. Our
team has developed AutoParis-X (APX), an innovative tool designed to streamline and enhance urine cytology
assessments, with the potential to significantly advance the diagnostic process, much like the impact of
automation on Pap smear screenings. By refining and validating APX across multiple settings, we aim to improve
bladder cancer diagnosis, ultimately benefiting patients with more accurate, cost-effective care and advancing
our understanding of this prevalent and recurrent disease.
